summary: A 1970 memo about time standards in the ARPANET, discussing how clocks might be used to measure and time events across the network. It carries a distribution list of the sites and people involved in the early network group.

eli5.summary: Computers far apart need to agree on what time it is, like friends comparing watches before a race.

subtitle: A one-paragraph request from SRI: how accurate should a network-wide clock be?

tldr.problem: SRI was about to install a relatively accurate real-time clock and did not know how good it needed to be for network jobs such as measuring delay.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC does not specify anything. It asks the other network sites for comments on Network time standards.
tldr.outcome: The text records only the question and its distribution list. It contains no answer, so it sets no standard.

today: RFC 28 is a status-Unknown early request for comments and has not been obsoleted or updated. It sets no standard, so it is a historical record of a question only.

sections.title: A Request for Comments
sections.content:
RFC 28, dated 13 January 1970 and written by Bill English of SRI, is a single short paragraph. SRI was about to install a relatively accurate real-time clock on its system.

Before choosing, the author wanted to hear from the rest of the network group about Network time standards, so the sites could decide together how good the clock should be.
sections.eli5: Someone is about to buy a clock and asks his friends how precise it should be, so everyone can agree.

sections.title: What the Clock Is For
sections.content:
The only use the RFC names is delay measurement. Measuring how long something takes to cross the network needs a clock, and the quality of the clock limits how good the measurement can be.

The RFC gives no figures, no required accuracy and no proposed method. It only says the answer to 'how good should our clock be' depends on what the network community wants from time standards.
sections.eli5: If you want to time a race, your stopwatch has to be good enough to tell who won. The note asks how good the stopwatch must be.

sections.title: Distribution and Outcome
sections.content:
The memo is addressed to the people who then made up the network group, and lists them with their sites: MIT, Utah, SDS, UCLA, MITRE, RAND, BB&N, Raytheon, ARPA, LL and UCSB.

There is no technical content beyond the request, so the RFC itself defines no time standard. Any replies are not part of this document.
sections.eli5: The note was handed to a list of friends at different places. Their answers are not in the note.
